description: Team "Print Me to the Moon" is a tight-knit collective of high school students who have shared a lifelong, deep-rooted passion for space exploration, aerospace logistics, and advanced engineering systems. Highly skilled and deeply immersed in coding, software development, and AI-driven data modeling, the team excels at building clean, high-performance analytical tools and computational frameworks.
summary: The main goal of this project is to find a place on Earth that closely resembles a target location on Mars, so that permanent base construction can be tested here before it is attempted there. We chose Gale Crater, which offers sulfate deposits, basaltic sand, a flat ancient lakebed and an equatorial location. To define its needs, we designed an ISRU-based concept using waterless sulfur-concrete bricks. We built an interactive Python simulation comparing building materials under Mars conditions; sulfur concrete performed best. We then gathered everything into a scroll-driven website that walks visitors from the base concept through ISRU and Gale Crater to autonomous printing and, finally, back to Earth and the Karapınar field scenario. The site also hosts the live simulation and the AHP and neural network results. Using these requirements, we evaluated the Konya–Karapınar Basin. Like Gale, it is a closed basin with a dried lakebed, gypsum deposits, volcanic basalt around Meke Lake, flat firm ground and large day–night temperature swings. Karapınar ranked second in the AHP, just behind Atacama. Because NASA already uses Atacama heavily, we chose Konya instead, an unexplored analog. Every step served one purpose: finding a high-fidelity Earth counterpart of Gale Crater.
details:
Print Me to Mars: ISRU Architecture & Terrestrial Analog Validation

What does it do or how does it work? "Print Me to Mars" is an end-to-end In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) construction architecture designed for building permanent Martian settlements, coupled with a comprehensive analytical model to validate terrestrial analog sites for testing.

The system operates by abandoning water-based concrete. Instead, autonomous rovers extract Martian sulfate minerals (abundant in Gale Crater) and thermochemically reduce them into elemental sulfur. This sulfur is mixed with local basaltic regolith (25-35% sulfur binder to 65-75% basalt aggregate) and melted at a highly efficient 115°C. Rather than extruding liquid walls that are prone to thermal shock, the system presses the mixture into interlocking (dry-stacked) modular bricks. To physically test this system on Earth, we utilized a multi-criteria decision-making model to identify the Konya Karapınar Basin in Türkiye as a high-fidelity terrestrial analog for Mars’ Gale Crater, mirroring its gypsum deposits, basaltic sands, and zero-slope dry lakebed topography.

What benefits does it have?

  1. Zero Water Waste: Traditional Portland cement requires water—a critical survival resource on Mars. Sulfur concrete cures without a single drop of water.
  2. Thermal Shock Resilience: Mars experiences extreme diurnal temperature swings exceeding 100°C. Rigid, mortar-based walls would suffer catastrophic fatigue and cracking. Our interlocking brick design incorporates millimeter-scale expansion joints, allowing the structure to safely expand and contract.
  3. Energy Efficiency: Melting sulfur requires significantly less energy than manufacturing traditional cement. The system utilizes optimized operating windows—running high-power heating phases during peak solar irradiance and utilizing passive Multi-Layer Insulation (MLI) to manage the thermal budget.

What is the intended impact of the project? The project provides a logistically independent blueprint for interplanetary colonization, eliminating the astronomical cost of transporting heavy construction materials from Earth. Furthermore, it introduces the Konya Karapınar Basin to the global space science community as a highly accurate, accessible, and mathematically validated Earth analog site for testing autonomous planetary robotics and ISRU logistics, paving the way for safer and more reliable Mars missions.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Python & Streamlit: We developed a custom, interactive web simulation application to evaluate planetary environmental parameters, simulate the thermal properties of different binders, and calculate energy budgets for ISRU manufacturing.
  • Machine Learning / Artificial Intelligence: We engineered an expert-prior single-layer Artificial Neural Network (ANN) using supervised learning to calibrate and independently verify our multi-criteria decision weights against 8 established terrestrial analog sites.
  • NASA Mars Trek: Used extensively for planetary mapping, analyzing MOLA Color Hillshade, Surface Roughness, Bound Water/Polyhydrated Sulfates, and Thermal Inertia layers of Gale Crater.
  • Analytical Tools: Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) mathematics for quantifying the multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) matrix. NOAA and Turkish Ministry climate/geological datasets for Earth analog comparisons.

How is your project creative? The creativity lies in turning a severe Martian limitation—extreme temperature fluctuation—into an architectural parameter. Instead of fighting thermal expansion, the mortarless interlocking brick design accommodates it. Additionally, our approach to finding an Earth analog was not based on mere visual similarity (like many red deserts). Instead, we reverse-engineered the search using a rigorous hybrid AHP-ANN mathematical model, strictly prioritizing the chemical (gypsum/basalt) and thermodynamic (diurnal temperature variations) requirements of sulfur concrete. We even mapped out a specific 70km logistical testing triangle in Karapınar (Meke Lake to Bahçeli) to simulate rover endurance and resource gathering.

What factors did your team consider? Our team evaluated a complex matrix of planetary and operational constraints:

  • Geology & Topography: We required a zero-slope closed basin with bedrock to prevent rover sinking and ensure 3D printer calibration, alongside adjacent deposits of both sulfates (binder) and basalt (aggregate).
  • Thermal Dynamics: We factored in solar incidence angles, night/day temperature deltas (ΔT), and freezing days to calculate the energy required to prevent thermal shock (cracking) during the controlled cooling (annealing) of the bricks.
  • Environmental Hazards: We accounted for the triboelectric charging of Martian dust, designing Electrodynamic Dust Shields (EDS) to keep solar panels functional without mechanical wipers, and factored in relative humidity limits for our terrestrial testing site.
